_comment: Applicability rules (CONTRACTS §8). Scope = requirement id, section id or chapter id; the most specific scope wins. Several rules with the same scope are OR-ed. A rule at requirement level inside a conditional chapter (for example V6 → auth) must repeat that condition, because it replaces the chapter rule. Reasons are written for a small-business owner.

rules.notApplicableReason: No OAuth or OpenID Connect: this app uses its own local accounts, not sign-in through another provider such as Google or Microsoft.
This app has no real-time audio or video calls (WebRTC).
This app does not issue self-contained tokens such as JWTs. Its API keys are opaque values that are checked against the database on every request.
This app does not accept file uploads or serve user files, so the file-handling requirements do not apply.
This app does not use GraphQL; its API uses plain JSON over fixed routes.
This app does not use WebSockets (live two-way connections); every request is a normal web request.
This app runs on this computer only, without HTTPS, so there is no HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect to configure.
rules.deploymentNote: When the app goes online behind a TLS proxy, only pages people open in a browser should redirect from HTTP to HTTPS; API routes should refuse plain HTTP instead.

Node's built-in web server handles request boundaries correctly. Once a load balancer or proxy is added in front of the app, ask the hosting provider to confirm it is kept up to date and does not disagree with the app about where a request ends (HTTP request smuggling).

rules.notApplicableReason: This app does not use an LDAP directory, so LDAP injection is not possible.
This app does not run XPath queries (it does not query XML documents).
This app does not process LaTeX documents.
This app has no rich-text (WYSIWYG) editor and never accepts HTML from users; all text is shown as plain text.
This app does not render Markdown, templates or stylesheets supplied by users; user text is always shown as plain text.
JNDI is a Java technology; this app is written in TypeScript for Node.js and does not use it.
This app does not use a memcache server; all data lives in its own SQLite database file.
Node.js does not have C-style format strings that user input could exploit.
This app does not send email, so there is no mail system that user input could reach.
This app is written in TypeScript, a memory-safe language, and contains no unmanaged (C/C++) code.
This app never parses XML documents, so XML external entity (XXE) attacks are not possible.
This app never serves files uploaded by users, so browsers cannot be tricked into interpreting a file as a web page.
This app runs on this computer only (loopback address, no HTTPS), so the 'Secure' cookie flag has no effect yet.
rules.deploymentNote: Before the app is reached over a network, run it in a TLS mode (behind an HTTPS proxy or with a certificate). The session cookie then automatically gets the Secure flag and the __Host- prefix.

rules.notApplicableReason: The __Host- cookie prefix only works over HTTPS, and this app runs on this computer only without HTTPS.
rules.deploymentNote: In a TLS mode the session cookie is renamed to __Host-sid automatically.

rules.notApplicableReason: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) tells browsers to insist on HTTPS. This app runs on this computer only without HTTPS, so the header would have no effect.
rules.deploymentNote: In a TLS mode the app sends Strict-Transport-Security with a one-year lifetime automatically.

rules.notApplicableReason: Cross-site request forgery protection defends signed-in users; this app has no sign-in and no sessions to abuse.
Cross-site request forgery protection defends signed-in users; this app has no sign-in and no sessions to abuse.
This is a single application on one address; there are no separate applications sharing a hostname.
The app's pages do not use the browser postMessage feature to talk to other windows or frames.
This app has no sign-in, so there are no accounts, passwords or login screens to protect.
Multi-factor authentication (a second step at sign-in, such as an authenticator app) only matters when people sign in; this app has no sign-in.
This app never sends one-time codes by phone call or text message (SMS). Its second sign-in step uses an authenticator app.
This app does not use out-of-band sign-in codes (codes sent by phone, SMS or push notification).
This app has no sign-in, so there are no sign-in codes to protect from guessing.
This app does not sign people in through an external identity provider (such as Google, Microsoft or a company single sign-on). It keeps its own accounts.
Sessions keep track of who is signed in; this app has no sign-in, so there are no sessions.
This app is not part of a single sign-on (SSO) setup with other systems.
This app does not sign people in through an external identity provider, so there is no federated re-authentication.
Ownership checks (only the person who created a record can open it) need sign-in; this app has no sign-in.
This app serves one organization. It does not host several separate customer organizations that must be kept apart from each other.
Password hashing only matters when there are passwords; this app has no sign-in.
Password hashing only matters when there are passwords; this app has no sign-in.
This app runs on this computer only (loopback address) without HTTPS, so there is no TLS connection to configure.
rules.deploymentNote: Before anyone reaches the app over a network, run it in a TLS mode: behind an HTTPS reverse proxy (recommended) or with its own certificate. Only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are then allowed.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app runs on this computer only (loopback address) without HTTPS, so there is no TLS connection to configure.
rules.deploymentNote: In the self-signed TLS mode the app allows TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. Behind a proxy, ask the hosting provider to confirm the same.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app runs on this computer only (loopback address) without HTTPS, so there is no TLS connection to configure.
rules.deploymentNote: In the self-signed TLS mode the app uses modern cipher suites only. Behind a proxy, ask the hosting provider to confirm the same.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app is not reachable from outside this computer and has no HTTPS yet, so there is no public connection to encrypt.
rules.deploymentNote: When the app goes online it must be served over HTTPS only, with a certificate from a trusted authority (for example Let's Encrypt through the hosting provider).

rules.notApplicableReason: This app does not talk to any other service over the network. Its database is a local file, so there is no connection between services to encrypt.
This app does not talk to any other service over the network. Its database is a local file, so there is no connection between services to encrypt.
rules.deploymentNote: Only outbound calls to other services are in scope here: the database is a local file, not a network connection. All outbound calls use HTTPS through the app's outbound client.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app does not talk to any other service over the network, so there are no server certificates to check.
This app is a single service with a local database file; there are no internal services talking to each other.
rules.deploymentNote: The app has no internal web services of its own; this only concerns the outbound calls it makes to other providers, which use HTTPS.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app is a single service with a local database file; there are no internal services with certificates to trust.
rules.deploymentNote: The app trusts only publicly trusted certificates for outbound calls; it never uses self-signed certificates for other services.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app is one program with a local database file; there are no separate backend components that need to authenticate to each other.
This app is one program with a local database file; there are no separate backend components running under their own accounts.
This app does not call other services over the network, so there are no outbound connections to time out.
This app does not call other services over the network, so there is no outbound traffic to restrict.
Clearing browser data at sign-out needs a sign-out; this app has no sign-in.
Cache rules for signed-in pages need sign-in; this app has no sign-in and shows no private pages.
This app does not call other services over the network, so there are no outbound redirects to control.
The safe-concurrency requirements are level 3 only, which is above the level this app targets.

rules.deploymentNote: On this computer the audit log is tamper-evident but stays on the same machine. Once the app is hosted online, ship its logs to a separate log service so an attacker who breaks in cannot erase their tracks.

rules.notApplicableReason: This app does not call other services over the network, so there are no outbound failures to handle.
This app does not train or fine-tune any AI model. It uses a ready-made model from a vendor, so training-data requirements do not apply.

A separate content-moderation check (for violence, self-harm, hate and sexual content) is not turned on for this assistant. The vendor's model has its own built-in safety rules. It can be turned on later with the AI_MODERATION setting.
A separate content-moderation check is not turned on for this assistant, so there is no classifier to test with other languages.
The assistant accepts typed text only; it does not take images, video or audio.
The AI model is hosted and maintained by the vendor (Anthropic). This app does not build, deploy or roll back models of its own.
The AI model runs on the vendor's own infrastructure, not on hardware this app controls, so infrastructure and hardware requirements sit with the vendor.
These requirements are level 3 only, which is above the level this app targets.
The assistant does not search a document store or vector database; it only reads app records through the signed-in user's own permissions.
The assistant does not use a retrieval pipeline or vector database, and nothing is stored inside a model.
The assistant cannot take actions, so there is no action-authorization component to isolate.
This app serves one organization; it does not host several separate customer organizations sharing the same assistant.
No model files are downloaded or imported; the model stays with the vendor and is used over its API.
No model files are downloaded or imported, so there are no model artifacts to integrity-check.
No model files are promoted between environments; the vendor-hosted model is pinned by name in the app's settings.
This app does not publish an AI bill of materials for model artifacts of its own; the model inventory is a generated document (docs/ai.md) and is not cryptographically signed.
There is no build step that assembles model artifacts, so there is no AI bill-of-materials check to fail the build.
A separate content-moderation check on the assistant's answers is not turned on. The vendor's model has its own built-in safety rules. It can be turned on later with the AI_MODERATION setting.
The assistant does not quote or cite retrieved documents, because it has no document store to retrieve from.
The assistant does not keep conversation history between visits and has no vector database, so there is no stored memory to protect.
There is no vector database; conversation history is plain rows in the app's own database, scoped to each user.
There is no document store with metadata tags; conversation history is plain rows in the app's own database.
The assistant does not keep conversation history between visits, so there is nothing to retrieve.
The assistant does not create embeddings or use a vector database.
The assistant does not keep conversation history between visits, so there is no memory to reset.
The assistant can only answer questions; it cannot create, change or delete anything, so there are no actions that need approval.
The assistant can only answer questions; it cannot create, change or delete anything, so there are no actions that need approval.
The assistant has no tools it can call, so there are no tools to isolate or authorize.
The assistant has no tools it can call, so there are no tool outputs to validate.
The assistant cannot install or invoke anything, so there are no external resources named by the model to check.
There is a single assistant, not several AI agents that need to identify each other.
The assistant cannot take actions on anyone's behalf, so there are no agent actions to authorize.
The assistant cannot take actions on anyone's behalf, so there are no agent actions to authorize.
The assistant does not use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to tools or servers.
The AI model is trained, calibrated and protected against copying by the vendor (Anthropic); this app cannot change how the model itself was built.
This app does not train any model, so there is no training on sensitive data to protect.
Separate anomaly detection on assistant inputs is not turned on for this app. Inputs are still screened for known prompt-injection patterns (see C2.1.3).
The assistant has no document retrieval step, so there are no retrieval events to log.
Model drift (the model's behavior changing over time) is monitored by the vendor that hosts the model; the app pins one model version by name.
The assistant cannot take actions on its own, so there is no proactive behavior to monitor.
This app does not train models or manage training data; the model's lifecycle is audited by the vendor.
SecureVibe does not fine-tune the AI model or run a feedback program that changes it; the model is the vendor's. Flagging a bad suggestion is done by editing your answers or the generated code.
SecureVibe does not generate infrastructure or pipeline configuration files (such as Terraform or CI workflows), so there is nothing for policy-as-code tools to check.
There is no CI/CD pipeline in a local build, so there are no pipeline trigger settings to protect.
There is no source-control server, branch protection or merge queue in a local build. SecureVibe enforces its own list of protected files in the tool layer instead (see AC.8.1).

There is no deployment pipeline that could check signed origin metadata; SecureVibe writes the app to a folder on this computer. It still records who generated what in securevibe.provenance.json (see AC.10).
There are no pull requests from outside contributors; the only code the AI reviews is the code it generated for you on this computer.
There is no CI/CD pipeline (no GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or similar) in a local build, so pipeline-hardening requirements do not apply.
This app receives no code contributions from outside people (no pull requests or forks), so there are no inbound contributions to screen.
